explication:
<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README contents, Upsonic is a Python-based, reliability-focused framework that enables trusted agent workflows for real-world applications. The architecture has a clear separation between client functionality (to create and manage tasks, agents, reliability layers, and integrations) and server functionality (to expose APIs, manage tool calls, and enforce reliability layers). It also integrates with external services (e.g., LLM providers and MCP tool servers) and supports advanced reliability patterns (like iterative verification, rounds, and loops).

Below are detailed guidelines for drawing an accurate and detailed system design diagram tailored to the Upsonic project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • Client Libraries and Modules:
     - Modules under src/upsonic/client (e.g., agent_configuration, direct_llm_call, multi_agent, markdown, tasks, knowledge_base, etc.).  
     - These modules encapsulate functionality like basic tasks, advanced agent workflows, task distribution, and direct LLM calls.
   • Server Components:
     - Modules under src/upsonic/server (including API definitions in api.py, level_one, level_two, level_utilized, storage, markdown, and others).
     - These components handle incoming requests, manage agent calls, verify outcomes, and ensure secure, reliable operation.
   • Tools Server:
     - The modules under src/upsonic/tools_server, including function_client, server API definitions, and associated server utilities.
     - This component acts as the entry point for tool integration and direct execution of MCP or Python-function based tools.
   • Reliability Layer:
     - Critical reliability mechanisms are embedded in both client and server modules (e.g., verifier agents, editor agents, rounds and loops).
     - These layers enforce verification and quality control on LLM output and overall agent responses.
   • Entry Points / Bootstrapping:
     - Files like run_main_server.py and run_tools_server.py indicate how the application is started.
   • Configuration and Deployment:
     - Dockerfile, pyproject.toml, and various GitHub workflows support testing, deployment, and continuous integration.

2. Define Relationships and Interactions:
   • Draw directional arrows to represent data flow:
     - Between the client components (agents, tasks, multi-agent systems) and the server APIs.
     - From client calls (such as direct LLM call modules) to external model providers (e.g., OpenAI/gpt-4o).
     - Communication between the Tools Server and both the Client and external MCP tool servers.
     - Within the reliability layer: show the iterative process where the verifier agent sends output to the editor agent for refinement.
   • Illustrate dependency flows:
     - How the high-level “Task” objects are processed by Agents, passed through reliability verification loops, and then executed by the underlying server or direct call modules.
     - Illustrate connections to external services (LLM providers, MCP servers, telemetry endpoints).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns & Design Principles:
   • Layered Architecture and Separation of Concerns:
     - Emphasize the clear division between presentation (client APIs/SDK), application logic (agent workflows and reliability mechanisms), and infrastructure (server endpoints, tool management, and external integrations).
   • Modular Design:
     - Indicate that the system is modular, with separate modules for various functionalities (e.g., call, storage, language, multi-agent distribution).
   • Fault Tolerance and Reliability:
     - Show the feedback loops (rounds and iterative editor corrections) that underpin the reliability features.
     - Highlight how the system’s reliability layer integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) and supports additional security via isolated runtime environments.

4. Include Relevant Technologies & Integration Points:
   • Python (with type hints and Pydantic for structured responses).
   • Docker (for containerized deployment).
   • External APIs: LLM providers like OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as MCP server support.
   • Cloud deployment options (AWS, GCP, etc.) as referenced in the documentation.
   • Telemetry system for anonymous usage data.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For this full-stack framework:
     - Clearly distinguish between the frontend (client SDK usage and agent workflow configuration) and the backend (server API endpoints, security runtimes, and reliability layers).
     - Emphasize that the framework supports real-time, production-ready applications through its layered reliability system.
     - Note integration points for third-party tool management and external computational calls.
   • Use shapes and colors:
     - For example, use rectangles for major components (Client, Server, Tools Server, External Services), distinct color coding for reliability layers, and directional arrows to show interactions.
     - Label components clearly with names such as “Client Agent Module”, “LLM Direct Call”, “Verification Layer”, “Server API”, “Tools Server”, etc.
   • Include callouts that indicate iterative workflows:
     - E.g., illustrate loops where the verifier agent sends feedback to the editor agent, and where agents handle multi-task coordination via the MultiAgent module.

6. Diagram Elements to Include:
   • Each component should be clearly labeled (Client, Server, Tools, Reliability Engine, External Integrations).
   • Directional arrows should show data flow (e.g., Tasks flow from the client to the server, server responses back to the client).
   • Use overlays or annotations to denote configuration and deployment artifacts (Dockerfile, CI/CD workflows, etc.).
   • Clearly demarcate the internal reliability processes (Verifier Agent, Editor Agent, Rounds, Loops).

By following these guidelines, the system design diagram will encapsulate the Upsonic architecture’s modularity, the separation of client and server responsibilities, the crucial reliability layer, and its support for external integrations. This detailed breakdown will help a principal software engineer grasp both the high-level flow and the individual components required to manage agent-based tasks with a strong emphasis on reliability.

Happy diagramming!
</explanation>
